questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
The choice was guided by how well the destination aligned with my Political Science programme, ensuring that I could take relevant courses and receive credit transfer. Access to a grant was also an important factor in making the exchange financially sustainable.

 I was also motivated by the opportunity to experience a different cultural context  then westeren Europe while still being based in the continent. Prague offered a balance between familiarity and newness, and its central location made it easy and affordable to travel across Europe , which I saw as an important part of the exchange experience.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was quite easy to find the information I needed. The university had very helpful advisors, and they organised several information sessions both before and after arrival. It felt like there was always someone to ask, and the process was clearly explained, which made settling in much easier.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I received support both online and in person. Before arriving, there was clear communication and guidance through online platforms, and once I got there, the university offered in person assistance through advisors and introduction sessions.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
I found housing through Facebook, mainly by connecting with people who seemed trustworthy and like a good fit to live with. It was relatively straightforward, but you do have to be a bit careful.

I would recommend taking your time to check profiles, have a short call if possible, and avoid anything that feels rushed or unclear. There are scams out there, so it is important not to send money before you are confident that everything is legitimate.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend living off campus. I did not hear many positive things about student housing, and having your own place or sharing with others in the city gives a much better overall experience.

Even though rent can be close to what you would pay in Copenhagen, where you live has a big impact on how you experience the city. I lived in Vinohrady in Prague 2, which was a great area and something I would really recommend.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The registration process took place online at a specific time, where all students signed up for courses at the same time. This made it quite competitive, so it was important to be ready when registration opened.

I would strongly recommend having a clear plan in advance, including backup options, so you know exactly which courses to choose. If you are not prepared, you risk not getting the courses you need for credit transfer at your home university.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There was support available through student counselling, where you could get guidance on course selection and administrative questions. It was also possible to speak directly with professors during their seminars. If a course was full, some professors were open to letting additional students join if you asked in person.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: It took some time and a bit of flexibility, but in the end I was able to register for all the courses I needed.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Have a clear plan for your courses in advance, especially if your home university requires specific courses for credit transfer. It is not something you can figure out on the spot during registration, so preparation really matters. It is also a good idea to work in teams with other students in the same situation. 

Also, don't lose hope. If you take it seriously, you will figure it out in the end <3

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The overall level of the courses felt manageable and in many ways less demanding than at my home university. The main challenge was not the academic level itself, but adapting to a different teaching style.

There was a stronger emphasis on presentations and continuous participation, and the structure of courses and how literature was approached felt quite different. It also takes some time to adjust to studying and presenting in English, but there was definitely room to make mistakes and learn along the way, which made the transition easier.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Attendance was taken, and classes were smaller, which meant that participation was more visible.

This also created a stronger sense that the professor was assessing you more individually, both in terms of engagement and performance throughout the course.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Democracy – Current Challenges and Innovations (5 ECTS)
EU Comparative Politics: Tensions in Representative Democracy (6 ECTS)
Introduction to History, Politics and Society of Russia and Eastern Europe (6 ECTS)
Current Central Asia: Building Autocracy for the 21st Century (6 ECTS)
Party Democracy in the EU: Crisis and Consequences (6 ECTS)
EU in Practice (6 ECTS)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend Democracy - Current Challenges and Innovations (5 ECTS). The course was very accessible and engaging.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Prague is generally affordable, which was great as it made it possible to eat out more often and travel around.

One thing I did not expect was related to rent. My landlord required payment for the full final month, even though I only stayed for half of it. In Copenhagen it is often possible to pay only for the time you actually stay, but that was not the case here. I would recommend clarifying this in advance.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Rent was more expensive than I expected, especially compared to other living costs in the city.

On the other hand, things like alcohol, food, and public transport were very affordable, which made everyday life and social activities much cheaper overall.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I did not personally take part in the Erasmus activities, but there were many options available for students. These included sports, social events and parties, organised trips, language courses, and different ways to explore the city. It seemed like there were plenty of opportunities to meet other students and get involved if you wanted to.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would strongly recommend taking the time to travel outside of Prague. The Czech Republic is incredibly beautiful and has many interesting destinations that are easy to reach, which adds a lot to the overall experience.

I would also recommend exploring the cultural life in Prague itself. The city has a rich cultural scene, with history, architecture, and local traditions that are worth engaging with beyond the university.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend exploring beyond Prague, especially smaller cities, cabins, and nature areas. There are many unique  places that are easy to reach and really worth seeing.

At the same time, Prague itself has a very lively weekend atmosphere, with lots of great bars and a strong nightlife. Thrift shops are also surprisingly good and very cheap, with many unique finds. I would also recommend visiting the local farmers markets by the river, where you can eat well and find vintage items at very reasonable prices.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was not always easy to build close connections with locals. However, I would strongly recommend being open to meeting people from other cultures. For me, that was a key part of having a rich exchange experience.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
You can still sense the historical legacy of communism in certain everyday interactions. For example, there is generally less of a service oriented mindset, and some older people do not speak English, which can make simple situations a bit more challenging.

Compared to Denmark, where friendliness towards strangers is more common, interactions can sometimes feel more distant. However, you quickly learn not to take it personally.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I especially appreciated the openness and friendliness among young people. They were genuinely kind and curious, and interactions felt relaxed and welcoming. Rather than any sense of attitude, there was a clear openness that made it easy to connect and have nice conversations.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Be prepared to deal with a fair amount of bureaucracy, both with UCPH and Charles University. It is manageable, but it requires lots of patience and staying on top of administrative details.

Take time to really explore Prague. It is a beautiful city with a lot to offer, and some of the best experiences come from walking around and discovering it at your own pace.

Finally, try not to fill your entire exchange with visits from home. It is great to share the experience with others, but it can take up a lot of time and energy. Giving yourself space to settle in and explore on your own makes the experience much more meaningful.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
ake the time to reflect on what this experience means to you. An exchange is something you give yourself, and there is no single right way to do it.

There are many paths you can follow and it is easy to just go along with what everyone else is doing, but it is worth being a bit intentional. Be open, but also make your own choices in a way that supports your personal growth beyond the academic and social part.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
The most rewarding part was realizing that I can build a life for myself in a different country. I learned that I am able to create something for myself even without my usual network around me.

At the same time, the experience gave me a new appreciation for Copenhagen. Being away made me more aware of what I value at home and helped me see my everyday life from a new perspective.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Missing home

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
